lesson_title: Two Envelopes: Income, Expenditure and the Household Budget
hook_text: Your payslip says R10 500. You will never touch R10 500. Here's where it actually goes.
clip_script: Take two envelopes. Every rand that comes IN this month gets written on the first one. Every rand that goes OUT gets written on the second. That is a budget — the rest is labelling. Now the payslip's first trick. It says ten thousand five hundred at the top. You will never hold that. Three pieces are carved off before it reaches you: tax, eight-forty. The unemployment fund, one-oh-five — one rand out of every hundred you earn. And five twenty-five into a pension for the person you'll be at sixty. That's one thousand four hundred and seventy gone, and nine thousand and thirty actually lands. THAT is the only number the in-envelope gets. Budgeting with the ten-five is cooking supper with meat you haven't bought yet. And here's the mistake that ruins the month: don't write "tax" on the out-envelope. It never came in, so it can't go out. Count it twice and the whole month quietly stops adding up. In minus out. Money left is a surplus. Money short is a deficit — and a deficit always gets paid by somebody.
visual_style: A kitchen table, two brown envelopes, banknotes sliding between them; a payslip with three visible pieces carved off the top figure before the remainder drops onto the first envelope.
mood: Warm and steady, like an older cousin walking you through the family money for the first time.
pacing: Calm setup on the envelopes, brisk through the three deductions, firm landing on surplus versus deficit.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and build a budget that survives a bad month.
